reason: The sources support 17 atomic claims across multiple independent sites, providing a mind-bending narrative about continent-sized alien planet remnants hidden deep inside Earth.
story: 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized planet named Theia smashed into our infant Earth. This wasn't a minor collision—it was a cataclysm that vaporized rock and changed our world forever. While scientists once believed the resulting debris formed the Moon over many months or years, new high-resolution simulations reveal it could have happened in just a few hours. But Theia didn’t entirely disappear into space. Two massive, continent-sized 'blobs' of alien rock are still buried 1,800 miles deep in Earth's mantle, sitting just above the core. Located beneath Africa and the Pacific Ocean, these anomalies are likely the iron-rich relics of Theia's mantle that sank during the impact. We aren't just orbiting with a moon made of debris; we are living on a planet that swallowed another world whole, with its ancient heart still hidden deep beneath our feet.
angle: Two continent-sized 'blobs' of the alien planet Theia are still buried deep inside Earth’s mantle today.

claims.claim: Theia was a planet roughly the size of Mars.
The collision between Theia and the proto-Earth occurred approximately 4.5 billion years ago.
The Moon was formed from the debris ejected during this giant impact.
Recent high-resolution simulations suggest the Moon may have formed in just a few hours rather than months or years.
Earth and the Moon share nearly identical chemical and isotopic signatures, implying a common origin.
Two continent-sized structures known as 'blobs' are buried deep within Earth's mantle.
These mantle blobs are located approximately 1,800 miles below the surface.
The blobs are positioned specifically beneath Africa and the Pacific Ocean.
Scientists have identified these anomalies as remnants of the planet Theia.
Theia's remnants are approximately 2% to 3.5% denser than the surrounding terrestrial mantle.
Theia's iron core likely fused with the Earth's core during the impact.
The Moon is deficient in iron and has a small core because it formed from ejected crust and mantle fragments.
Theia may have been the source of much of Earth's water.
Theia's mass was estimated to be roughly 5% to 15% of Earth's modern mass.
The proto-Earth was nearly finished forming at the time of the Theia impact.
The deep-mantle anomalies are scientifically known as large low-velocity provinces (LLVPs).
The impact likely melted the upper half of the Earth's mantle.

disputed: The angle of impact is debated; early models suggested a glancing blow, while 2016 analyses suggest a direct head-on collision (attribute to scientific shift) [S1, S2].
The speed of Moon formation is disputed; traditional theories suggest months or years, while 2022 high-resolution simulations suggest it took only hours (attribute to new simulation data) [S2, S3].
Theia's origin is disputed; it may have formed in a stable Lagrange point near Earth or migrated from the outer solar system (attribute to different isotopic studies) [S1, S5].
